An allusion to Meng Jia, an official of the Jin dynasty (265-420), whose hat was blown off by the wind at a Double Ninth party and who did not notice. Du Fu turns it round: he is too self-conscious about his thinning hair to risk it.

glossary.en: qian - 'to ask, to beg a favour'
glossary.note: Here it means to ask someone politely to do something.
A fragrant plant worn in the hair or on the sleeve at the Double Ninth to ward off evil.
Another name for the Lantian mountains, which were known for their jade.

jiurilantiancuishizhuang.background: By Du Fu. It was probably written at this Double Ninth gathering at the Cui estate in Lantian during the Qianyuan era (758-760).

qiusi.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem by Lu You, set in autumn. He compares the world, driven by greed, to fire-oxen on the charge, and himself to a lone sand gull drifting on rivers and lakes. On an autumn night he hears the fulling mallets and sees the paulownia leaves fall, wishes for a high place to climb, and thinks of Chen Deng's hundred-foot tower. It voices the loneliness of his retirement and ambitions never fulfilled.

glossary.note: An allusion to Tian Dan of the Warring States kingdom of Qi, who broke a siege by tying torches to the tails of oxen and driving them at the enemy. Lu You uses it for people stampeded by greed.
The stone block and wooden club used to beat cloth. In autumn women pounded cloth to make winter clothes, and the sound stood for the season.

glossary.en: Yuanlong bai chi lou - 'Yuanlong's hundred-foot tower'
glossary.note: Chen Deng, courtesy name Yuanlong, of the Three Kingdoms period, is said to have remarked that he would lie high up in a hundred-foot tower and let everyone else lie on the floor. It stands for a lofty, wide-ranging outlook.

glossary.en: shu lao yan - 'to stretch old eyes'
glossary.note: To give his old eyes a wider view.

glossary.en: lang ji - 'to wander without a fixed course'
glossary.note: To drift from place to place, without settling.

qiusi.background: By Lu You (1125-1210), a Southern Song poet. He wrote it in his later years of retirement at Shanyin (today's Shaoxing).

zhanganqiuwang.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem on an autumn dawn in Chang'an: clouds drifting, palaces trembling in the high autumn air, stars fading, geese crossing, a flute, a chrysanthemum hedge, lotuses on a sandbar - all touched with autumn sorrow. It ends thinking of the perch he cannot go home for, wearing the southern cap in vain like the Chu prisoner. He is a traveller who cannot return.
zhanganqiuwang.translation:
Clouds and scenery drift cold and desolate, brushing the dawn;
The palaces and towers of Han shiver in the high autumn.
A few last stars; wild geese slant across the frontier.
One long note of a flute; someone leans on the tower.
Purple blooms half open, the hedge chrysanthemums are still;
The red robes are all fallen, and the lotuses on the islet grieve.
The perch is at its best, yet I do not go home -
Wearing a southern cap for nothing, playing the Chu prisoner.

glossary.note: The clouds and the sights below them.

glossary.en: Han jia gong que - 'palaces of Han'
glossary.note: A poet of the Tang often wrote 'Han' for his own dynasty. Here it means the palaces of Chang'an under the Tang.
Lotuses growing beside a small sandbar in the water.

glossary.en: lu yu zheng mei - 'the perch is at its best'
glossary.note: An allusion to Zhang Han of the Western Jin. When the autumn wind rose he thought of the perch and water-shield soup of his home in Wu, resigned and went home.

glossary.en: nan guan Chu qiu - 'southern cap, the Chu prisoner'
glossary.note: Zhong Yi, a man of the state of Chu, was taken prisoner in the Spring and Autumn period but still wore his southern cap. It stands for someone abroad who remembers his own country.

zhanganqiuwang.background: By Zhao Gu, a late Tang poet. The poet Du Mu admired the line about the flute and the man leaning on the tower so much that people called Zhao 'Zhao Who Leans on the Tower'.

dalidan.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem, Wei Yingwu's reply to his friend Li Dan. The first four lines recall parting last year among the flowers and another year gone, with life hard to foresee and spring sorrow in sleepless nights. The last four say he is ill and thinks of the countryside, ashamed of his salary because refugees fill his district, and that on hearing his friend means to visit he has watched the moon from the west tower many times.

glossary.note: A friend of Wei Yingwu, courtesy name Yuanxi.
Describes a low, gloomy state of mind.
The countryside and the home village, a life away from office.
People leaving home because of famine or harsh government.
The pay of an official.

glossary.en: wen xun - 'to ask after, to call on'
glossary.note: To visit and enquire how someone is.

dalidan.background: By Wei Yingwu, a Tang poet. He was then prefect of Chuzhou (in today's Anhui).

oucheng.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem by a Neo-Confucian philosopher, expressing leisure and quiet contentment. Watching things calmly, he sees each at home in its place, and the pleasures of the seasons are shared with all. It ends encouraging himself with the idea of 'wealth does not lead astray, poverty brings joy': a person who reaches this point is a hero. It is one of the best known philosophical poems of the Song.

glossary.note: A poem that came about by chance, without any set occasion.
Each thing finds its own place and is at ease there.
A fine, happy frame of mind.

glossary.en: dao tong tian di you xing wai - 'the Dao runs through heaven and earth, beyond form'
glossary.note: The Dao (the Way) joins heaven and earth together and goes beyond things that have shape.

glossary.en: fu gui bu yin pin jian le - 'wealth does not lead astray, poverty brings joy'
glossary.note: It is adapted from Mencius, who says that wealth and rank cannot lead one astray and poverty and lowliness cannot shake one. Cheng Hao changes the second part to say that poverty brings joy.

oucheng.background: By Cheng Hao (1032-1085), a Neo-Confucian philosopher of the Northern Song.

chunxilvhuai.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem of homesickness, written as a traveller in the land of Chu in late spring. Flowing water and falling flowers are heartless, home is ten thousand li away in a butterfly dream, the cuckoo cries at the third watch, family letters are long cut off and white hair has come. It ends with wry self-mockery: he could go home whenever he wished, and no one is contesting the misty Five Lakes.

glossary.note: A walled city in the old land of Chu, around the middle Yangtze.
An allusion to Zhuangzi, who dreamed he was a butterfly and could not tell afterwards whether he was a man who had dreamed of a butterfly. Here it just means a dream.
Legend says the spirit of Du Yu, a ruler of Shu, became the cuckoo, whose call sounds like 'better go home'.
Hair that is going grey.
A general name for the lakes and rivers where hermits retire. Legend has Fan Li, after his achievements, sailing away on them.

chunxilvhuai.background: By Cui Tu, a late Tang poet who spent his life travelling.

dadingyuanzhen.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem, Ouyang Xiu's reply to a friend, Ding Yuanzhen, while he was demoted to Yiling. In the mountain town it is still cold in the second month, with snow on the branches and frozen thunder startling the bamboo shoots. At night he hears wild geese and is homesick, and is ill as the new year begins. He comforts himself: once a flower-viewer in Luoyang, he need not sigh if the wild flowers come late. It is understated and broad-minded.

glossary.note: Ding Baochen, whose courtesy name was Yuanzhen, a friend of Ouyang Xiu.

glossary.en: tian ya - 'the ends of the earth'
glossary.note: The edge of the sky. Here it means Yiling, a remote place.
Thunder that comes in the cold of early spring.

glossary.en: wu hua - 'the beauty of the scenery'
glossary.note: The fine things of nature, the sights of a season.

glossary.en: Luoyang hua xia ke - 'a guest among the flowers of Luoyang'
glossary.note: Ouyang Xiu served in Luoyang in his early career and enjoyed its tree peonies. Here he is speaking of himself.

dadingyuanzhen.background: By Ouyang Xiu (1007-1072), a Northern Song writer and statesman. He wrote it during the Jingyou era (1034-1038) when he was demoted to magistrate of Yiling (today's Yichang in Hubei).

qingmingriduijiu.summary: An eight-line seven-syllable regulated poem about what the poet sees at Qingming, the grave-sweeping festival: graveyards on every hilltop, paper ash drifting like white butterflies, azaleas dyed with tears of blood, foxes asleep on tombs at sunset and children laughing by the lamp at night. It ends bluntly: while there is wine, get drunk, because not one drop reaches the Nine Springs. The contrasts are stark and show a clear view of life and death.

glossary.note: Land set aside for graves.

glossary.en: ji sao - 'to make offerings and sweep the grave'
glossary.note: The Qingming custom of tidying a grave and offering food, wine and paper money.
The ash of burnt paper money, blown up like white butterflies. The last character is a variant of the usual one for 'butterfly'.
It can mean the azalea flower, or the cuckoo of legend that cries until it spits blood. Both images are in the line.
The Yellow Springs, the underworld where the dead are.

qingmingriduijiu.background: By Gao Zhu, a Southern Song poet of the 'Rivers and Lakes' group, wandering poets who did not hold high office.
